analysis.one_liner: Taxes large employers the full value of federal aid their workers receive, like food stamps and Medicaid.
analysis.headline: A single senator introduced the bill with no cosponsors; it never got a hearing, markup, or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies with 500 or more employees would owe the Treasury a tax equal to 100% of the food stamps, school meals, housing assistance, and Medicaid their employees receive. The idea is to make big employers either pay the cost of low wages directly or raise pay enough that workers don't need public aid. It would also make it illegal for those companies to ask job applicants whether they receive federal benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers at very large companies, who would gain either higher pay or benefits if their employer chose to avoid the new tax, and taxpayers generally, who would stop subsidizing the payrolls of companies whose workers still qualify for aid.

how_it_helps.text: A company with at least 500 employees would owe a tax equal to 100% of the SNAP (food stamp), school lunch and breakfast, Section 8 housing, and Medicaid benefits its employees and their dependents receive for the year, giving it a direct financial reason to raise pay or benefits above eligibility levels.

The tax counts full-time and part-time employees and also independent contractors unless they meet a strict independence test, so a company could not escape it simply by relabeling its workforce as contractors.

Large employers could not ask applicants whether they receive federal benefits; a violation would be enforced by the Labor Department and carry lost wages plus an equal amount of liquidated damages for the applicant.

analysis.who_pays: Very large employers with substantial numbers of workers on public assistance — big retailers, fast food chains, and warehouse and delivery companies — who would owe the tax unless they raised wages enough to move workers off benefit rolls.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large retail, fast food and warehouse chains

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every dollar of aid an employee's household receives, for any reason — family size, disability, or state eligibility — not just aid tied to low wages, which could make companies reluctant to hire people from low-income households at all.
Because Medicaid payments are large, the bill's dollar exposure for a big employer could be enormous, and an employer might respond by cutting hours or positions rather than raising pay.

Employers could avoid the tax by keeping workers' pay just above benefit eligibility lines or shifting jobs to smaller subsidiary companies, limits on which the bill only partially addresses through its employer-aggregation rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: workers at very profitable large companies qualify for food stamps and Medicaid because their pay is low, and taxpayers pick up the difference. But it is a blunt instrument. The tax counts all benefits a household receives regardless of why, which could discourage the hiring of people from low-income families — the very people it aims to help — and its Medicaid-based exposure is so large that companies might cut jobs rather than raise wages. A bill designed to pressure wage growth would have worked better aimed specifically at pay below benefit-eligibility levels.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing further ever happened to it before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced S. 3410 on September 5, 2018; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee that same day.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the action history shows no activity after the referral, and the Congress ended January 3, 2019.
The bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so it carried no visible Senate support beyond its single sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers whose workers rely on food stamps, Medicaid, and housing aid avoided a new tax equal to those benefits and the wage pressure that came with it. Workers' benefit levels and taxpayers' subsidy bills stayed exactly as they were.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it received no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Amazon
against.role: Large employer targeted in the public debate over the bill
against.what_they_did: Publicly disputed the senator's claims about its wages and workers' benefit use after he highlighted the company when promoting the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split was recorded; the bill had a single independent sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Large low-wage employers (retail, fast food, warehousing and delivery)
industries.note: These companies would owe a tax equal to the SNAP, school meals, housing, and Medicaid benefits their employees receive — a direct cost unless wages rise enough to move workers off aid. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the low-wage workers it was meant to help.

Independent contractors count as employees under the bill unless they meet a strict independence test, so platforms could not sidestep the tax by keeping workers classified as contractors. Contracting arrangements are often cheaper precisely because they shift costs onto workers.

industries.industry: Government benefits programs (SNAP, school meals, Section 8, Medicaid)
industries.note: The programs themselves are not cut; the bill simply makes employers reimburse the Treasury for the benefits their workers receive. Spending through these programs would fall only if employers raised pay — the intended result.
